title: Closest Accessible Symmetry reduction: a tool for Hamiltonian interpolation analysis
authors: Ana Palacios, Artur Garcia-Saez, Arnau Riera, Marta P. Estarellas
abstract: We introduce a framework for analysing the spectrum of Hamiltonian interpolations without heavily relying on discretising the interpolation parameter. The method is based on the concept of accessible symmetries: a problem-class-dependent family of certifiable reflections that induce bipartitions of the Hilbert space. At each step, the interpolation Hamiltonian is projected onto the sectors of the accessible symmetry that is closest to being satisfied, yielding a hierarchy of weakly coupled pseudo-eigenspaces together with explicit residual couplings between them. We show that this representation captures qualitative signatures of quantum phase transitions, provides estimates of their location, and offers insights into their nature. The quality of the approximation is controlled by the compatibility between the accessible symmetry family and the problem instance. Although motivated in spirit by adiabatic quantum computation, our approach applies more broadly to the study of Hamiltonian phase diagrams, providing a new perspective on the spectral reorganisation of many-body quantum systems.
summary: The paper introduces the Closest Accessible Symmetry (CAS) reduction method to analyze how the energy spectrum of many-body quantum systems changes during Hamiltonian interpolation. By systematically projecting the system onto symmetry-constrained subspaces, it avoids numerical discretization while accurately predicting critical points and characterizing phase transitions via pseudo-spectra and hybridization analysis.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a systematic framework for analyzing the energy spectrum of Hamiltonian interpolations between two Hamiltonians without relying on discretizing the interpolation parameter.
main_result: The Closest Accessible Symmetry (CAS) reduction provides a hierarchical, non-discretized method to approximate the pseudo-spectrum and locate quantum phase transitions by tracking spectral reorganization across the entire path.
method: The core technique involves projecting the interpolating Hamiltonian onto subspaces defined by accessible symmetries, yielding weakly coupled pseudo-eigenspaces whose coupling strengths are analyzed using hybridization criteria.
model_or_system: The analysis is applied to general many-body quantum systems undergoing adiabatic evolution, exemplified by the frustrated Ising ring model and linear interpolations between Hamiltonians A and B.
key_observables: Quantum phase transition locations (gap closing), pseudo-spectrum $\{\mu_k\}$, hybridization strength $\chi_{kj}$, and spectral gap bounds ($\Delta$ vs. $	ilde{\Delta}$).
important_parameters: The interpolation parameter $s \in [0, 1]$, the structure of accessible symmetries (e.g., single-Pauli string symmetries), and the cost function used to select the optimal symmetry reduction.
main_assumptions: The quality of the approximation depends on the compatibility between the chosen accessible symmetry family and the physical problem instance; the method relies on restricting the search space to tractable symmetry generators.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how different types of symmetries ($\mathbb{Z}_2$) can be generated by removing terms from $H(s)$, show fidelity comparisons between pseudo-eigenstates and true eigenstates, and plot spectral gap behavior across phase transitions for the Ising model.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the CAS framework, details its application to linear interpolations using symmetry constraints (Types I-IV), develops diagnostic tools like hybridization criteria ($\chi_{kj}$), and compares different optimization strategies (max-cost vs. average cost) on benchmark models.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful theoretical tool for analyzing quantum dynamics across phase transitions, offering insights into spectral reorganization that are complementary to standard time-stepping or local approximation methods.
